analysis.one_liner: Requires federal regulators to reject wholesale electricity rate increases that would push consumer bills up 5% or more.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Energy Committee with no hearing, vote, or further action since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Federal Power Act, the law governing wholesale electricity rates, to add consumer affordability as a factor the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) must weigh when deciding whether a rate is 'just and reasonable.' FERC would have to presume a rate change is unaffordable if it is likely to raise retail electricity prices by 5% or more, and an unaffordable rate could not be approved. In practice, this would give consumers a formal seat in the rate-review process and make it harder for utilities to pass large cost increases on to households.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electricity bills. Any electric customer in the regions where FERC-approved wholesale rates flow through to retail bills would gain a new protection: a rate hike large enough to raise their bill 5% or more would face a presumption of being unaffordable and could be rejected. The benefit is largest for people on tight budgets, for whom a 5% utility bill increase is a real hardship, and for parts of the country where wholesale rate cases have driven sharp bill increases.

how_it_helps.text: Requires FERC to consider whether an approved rate is likely to produce retail electricity prices that are unaffordable for consumers, a factor the Federal Power Act does not currently require. [S2]
Creates an automatic presumption that a rate is unaffordable if it would raise retail electricity prices by 5% or more, and bars FERC from treating such a rate as just and reasonable. [S2]
Uses the consumer definition already in the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act, tying the affordability test to actual electric consumers rather than abstract ratepayer categories. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities and wholesale power sellers, whose rate increases would face a new affordability hurdle before FERC. Utilities that want to recover large cost increases through rates — whether from fuel costs, grid upgrades, or new infrastructure — would have to justify them under the affordability test or absorb, restructure, or spread the costs. Ratepayer advocates generally see this cost as a shift of risk back onto companies and their investors rather than onto households.

drawbacks.text: A blanket 5% presumption could block rate increases that are legitimate — for example, recovering the cost of transmission upgrades, reliability work, or fuel price spikes that utilities do not control — potentially making it harder to finance grid investment. [S2]

FERC regulates wholesale rates while retail electricity prices are largely set by state regulators, so tying federal approval of a wholesale rate to predicted retail outcomes creates an enforcement mechanism that reaches into an area states traditionally control. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is a hard backstop against large bill increases at the federal level, which matters because electricity is an unavoidable expense. The cost falls on utilities and their investors, though an honest reading is that a rigid 5% trigger could also constrain needed grid investment, and the benefits would show up only in regions where FERC-jurisdictional rates actually drive retail bills. The design is simple and consumer-focused but blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has not taken it up.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on August 6, 2026. [S1]
No senators signed on as cosponsors. [S3]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities and wholesale power sellers are better off so far, since the affordability restriction has not moved and cannot constrain their rate filings while it sits in committee. Consumers gain nothing until the bill actually passes, which with no cosponsors and no committee action it shows no sign of doing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities; the bill has not advanced

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the Affordable Electricity Rates Act of 2026.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: There are no votes or opposing statements in the record; the only visible signals are a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and a Republican-run committee that has not acted.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and wholesale power sellers
industries.note: The bill adds an affordability test that presumes any wholesale rate likely to raise retail bills 5% or more is unaffordable and cannot be approved, directly limiting utilities' ability to increase revenue through rates. Because utilities profit by charging customers more, their interest in this bill runs against the consumers it protects.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since the August 2026 referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or floor vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
